added_rows.relationship: Same-chapter joint address and prescribed priestly examination
added_rows.rationale: The address to Moses and Aaron introduces the case of a skin mark brought to Aaron or his priestly sons for examination and a stated uncleanness verdict. The following clauses supply the particular persons and task attached to this speech.

added_rows.relationship: Same-chapter extensive white-skin condition and its examination verdict
added_rows.rationale: This clause describes leprosy covering the lesion's skin from head to foot in the priest's view; the next requires examination and declares clean when it has covered the body's skin and all turned white. The verdict is retained with its stated all-white condition.

added_rows.relationship: Same-chapter return-to-white condition and priestly reassessment
added_rows.rationale: This clause sends the person back to the priest if the sound skin is restored and turns white; the next commands examination and a clean verdict if the lesion has turned white. The paired clauses give the condition and its particular reassessment.

added_rows.relationship: Same-chapter whitish-patch case and its stated classification
added_rows.rationale: The man-or-woman case introduces shining whitish body patches; the next clause requires examination, calls the appearance a white eruption and declares clean. This connects the specified appearance to its actual stated verdict without importing another edition's description.

added_rows.relationship: Related leprosy uncleanness and an additional priestly food restriction
added_rows.rationale: The later law explicitly names leprosy as a condition barring Aaron's descendants from holy food until cleansing. This verse calls the affected person unclean and specifies garments, uncovered head and mouth covering, retaining its public-status directions beside that particular priestly restriction.

added_rows.relationship: Same-chapter speech introduction and the healed person's priestly examination
added_rows.rationale: The speech to Moses introduces the law for a person with leprosy on his cleansing day, brought to a priest who examines him outside camp for healing. These clauses supply the introduced speech's particular person, occasion, location and task.

added_rows.relationship: Same-chapter joint address and the landed-house examination instructions
added_rows.rationale: The address to Moses and Aaron introduces the Canaanite-land house case, the owner's report and the priest's command to empty the house before examination. The target gives the particular setting and procedure introduced by this speech.

added_rows.relationship: Same-chapter replacement materials after the prescribed removal
added_rows.rationale: The earlier directions remove affected stones and scrape the house, disposing of stones and dust outside the city in an unclean place. This clause then replaces those stones and uses other earth for plaster, giving a particular repair counterpart to that removal.

resolved_peer_corrections.issue: The rationale generalizes prepared with oil or not so prepared into prepared or unprepared offerings, losing the stated oil condition.
resolved_peer_corrections.required_rationale: Both assign the grain-sacrifice remainder to Aaron's sons; this verse specifies an equal share for each in offerings prepared with oil or not so prepared.

resolved_peer_corrections.issue: The rationale says both offerings use unleavened loaves, but the supplied Leviticus 7:12 explicitly applies unleavened only to its wafers.
resolved_peer_corrections.required_rationale: Both offerings name loaves prepared with oil and unleavened wafers spread with oil; the earlier law explicitly calls its loaves unleavened, while here the bread accompanies a sacrifice of praise.

resolved_peer_corrections.issue: Likewise comes with unleavened loaves can imply that Leviticus 7:12 expressly calls its loaves unleavened; distinguish the shared materials from Numbers' explicitly unleavened basket.
resolved_peer_corrections.required_rationale: The vow-completion deliverance ram likewise comes with oil-prepared loaves and unleavened wafers spread with oil; Numbers explicitly calls its basket bread unleavened, and its occasion is completion of a vow rather than the praise offering named here.

resolved_peer_corrections.issue: The rationale calls both passages an approach to holy food, whereas the target expressly has the broader consecrated holy things.
resolved_peer_corrections.required_rationale: Both attach a serious sanction to uncleanness in relation to what belongs to the Lord: eating deliverance meat here, and approaching consecrated holy things by the priestly seed in the later rule.

resolved_peer_corrections.issue: The rationale calls both washed parts entrails, replacing the source's supplied belly wording.
resolved_peer_corrections.required_rationale: Both rites wash the named belly or entrails and the feet with water before placing the whole flock offering on the altar as a sweet savour to the Lord; this account says belly and the earlier law says entrails.

old.rationale: Both assign the grain-sacrifice remainder to Aaron's sons; this verse specifies an equal share for each in the prepared or unprepared offerings it describes.

new.rationale: Both assign the grain-sacrifice remainder to Aaron's sons; this verse specifies an equal share for each in the offerings with or without oil.

old.rationale: Both offerings use unleavened loaves made with oil and wafers spread with oil; here the bread accompanies a sacrifice of praise.

new.rationale: Both offerings use fine-flour loaves prepared with oil and unleavened wafers spread with oil. The earlier grain law explicitly calls its loaves unleavened as well; this praise-offering verse explicitly applies that description to the wafers.

old.rationale: The vow-completion deliverance ram likewise comes with unleavened loaves prepared with oil and wafers spread with oil; its occasion is completion of a vow rather than the praise offering named here.

new.rationale: Both praise and vow-completion deliverance offerings include oil-prepared fine-flour loaves and unleavened wafers spread with oil. Numbers explicitly describes a basket of unleavened bread accompanying the ram, while this praise-offering verse explicitly calls the wafers unleavened.

old.rationale: Both threaten exclusion for approaching the Lord's holy food while personal uncleanness remains; here the act is eating deliverance meat, whereas the later rule addresses the priestly seed.

new.rationale: Both threaten exclusion while personal uncleanness remains, but the prohibited acts and recipients differ: eating the Lord's deliverance meat here, and the priestly seed approaching Israel's consecrated holy things in the later rule.

old.rationale: Both require washing the entrails and feet and placing the whole flock offering on the altar as a sweet savour to the Lord.

new.rationale: Both rites wash the feet with water and place the whole offering on the altar as a sweet savour. This consecration account names the ram's belly, while the flock whole-burnt law names the entrails; Moses acts here and the priest acts in the general law.
